issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Sovan, a 44-year-old Southeast Asian nurse, was walking to his car after a night shift when he was grabbed from behind, a knife pressed against his ribs, and his wallet and phone were taken. The attacker’s face was inches from his own, and he can still see it in perfect photographic detail—the scar above the brow, the yellowed teeth—as if the image were developed in his mind’s darkroom. Every time the memory returns, he feels a sharp, stabbing pain in his ribs exactly where the blade had been, even though there was no wound. In the weeks that followed, Sovan became convinced that something about him had made the attack happen—he had walked too slowly, or looked weak, or chosen the wrong route. This feeling of an intrinsic fault settled into a broader hopelessness: nothing good could ever come his way again, and his future had been stolen along with his phone. That same belief—that he was already marked for misfortune—meant that every unfamiliar face he passed in the hospital corridor carried a weight of potential danger, as though the world were simply waiting to prove him right. That same conviction—that he carried a visible flaw—kept dragging him back to the mugger’s face, as if the memory held the answer to what the attacker had seen in him.

Because he believed the attack was his own doing, Sovan began scanning every environment for clues he might have missed. At the hospital, he constantly peers around corners and checks behind supply carts before entering a room. He also catches himself looking in mirrors—the bathroom mirror, the reflective surface of the break-room microwave—searching his own face for whatever vulnerability the attacker had seen. He tells himself this vigilance will prevent another mistake, but the checking itself seems to summon the memory: the flash of silver, the grunt in his ear. The more he scans, the more the visual images intrude, and the more the pain flares in his ribs.

To keep his mind occupied, Sovan listens to podcasts constantly during his shifts and while driving. He finds that any silence invites the memory, so he fills every gap with noise. Yet the distraction fails in moments of unguarded stillness—when he wakes at 3 a.m. and stares at the ceiling, sleep shattered by a sound that was probably a car door. His sleep problems stem from a deep, wordless sense that he is never truly safe, that the mugger could be anywhere. On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay—it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome. During his commute, he constantly looks behind him, twisting his neck to scan the back seat of his own car, then the sidewalk as he walks. In the hospital cafeteria, he always chooses a seat with his back to the wall, and if that seat is taken, he leaves rather than sit exposed. The safe-seat seeking feels urgent, but it reinforces his belief that danger is pervasive and he is helpless to prevent it.

The threat he perceives also feeds back into his negative appraisals. Each time he checks behind him and feels a spike of fear, he thinks, See? Nothing good can happen to me now. The mugging has not only stolen the future he imagined—it has made him someone who expects pain at every turn. And the more hopeless he feels, the more he relies on his maladaptive strategies: the mirror checks, the mental noise, the constant scanning. They are his only way to manage the certainty that he is marked, that his intrinsic flaw will attract another attack.

One afternoon, while restocking supply cabinets, Sovan’s reflection startled him in the glass pane of a locked narcotics drawer. He froze, and the pain in his ribs returned so vividly that he dropped a box of syringes. A coworker asked if he was okay; he said he was fine, but later, alone in the locker room, he caught himself whispering, “I have no future.” This moment—the collision of the visual memory, the physical pain, and the hopeless appraisal—finally pushed him to seek help. He came to therapy because he is terrified that his constant vigilance is making him a worse nurse, that he will miss something real while searching for shadows. He hopes, doubtfully, that maybe there is a way to stop looking over his shoulder without being caught off guard.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals directly cause or influence the intrusive memory; instead, memory triggers appraisals, and appraisals lead to maladaptive behaviors that in turn trigger memory.
The vignette does not show that perceived threat directly causes memory intrusions; rather, threat leads to maladaptive strategies which may trigger memory, but no direct causal link is expressed.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals directly cause or influence the intrusive memory; instead, memory triggers appraisals, and appraisals lead to maladaptive behaviors that in turn trigger memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not show that perceived threat directly causes memory intrusions; rather, threat leads to maladaptive strategies which may trigger memory, but no direct causal link is expressed.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
